topic: Phillips curve, the Friedman-Phelps long-run critique, natural rate of unemployment and NAIRU

concepts.prereq_recalled: natural rate of unemployment; monetary and fiscal policy

book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook draws the short-run curve and the vertical long-run curve and defines NAIRU. Here the topic is told as the life of an idea: a provocative quote, the man and his data, his claim read on the curve, its fame, the challenge by two later economists, their reason, and the new term their challenge left behind. The learner first believes the trade-off, then watches it break on the same curve, and the natural rate is defined only when the dot needs a place to stop.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Follow the idea's life story: who claimed it, what the claim means on the graph, who challenged it and why, and what new term the challenge produced.

opening.what: A provocative quote over a crowd labelled UNEMPLOYMENT: the problem troubles most countries, yet its solution is small, as Bill Phillips claimed.

moves.what: He showed a stable inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment, drawn as a graph called the Phillips curve.

moves.concept: reading the curve: the trade-off

moves.concept: reading the curve: the trade-off
moves.what: If we raise inflation a little, unemployment falls; raise it more and unemployment falls a lot.

moves.concept: reading the curve: the trade-off
moves.what: Points at the graph: as soon as inflation was raised, unemployment dropped sharply.

moves.concept: reading the curve: the trade-off
moves.what: Phillips' claim: a slightly higher inflation can buy a permanent cut in unemployment.

moves.concept: reading the curve: the trade-off
moves.what: So the Phillips curve shows a trade-off between unemployment and inflation.

moves.concept: the curve's rise to fame
moves.what: Published in 1958 in Economica; in the 1960s it became the most popular theory among economists.

moves.concept: critique: the trade-off holds only in the short term
moves.what: But in the early 1970s Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps challenged it: valid only in the short term.

moves.concept: critique: the trade-off holds only in the short term
moves.what: You cannot keep unemployment low for long by raising inflation; in the long term unemployment starts rising.

moves.concept: why it breaks: wage demands lead to firing
moves.what: Very high inflation raises people's expenses, so sooner or later they demand higher wages; firms cannot raise everyone's pay; they let go the people they need least.

moves.concept: natural rate of unemployment
moves.what: The level where unemployment settles is the natural rate of unemployment (named before it is explained).

moves.concept: natural rate of unemployment
moves.what: So what actually is this natural rate?

moves.concept: natural rate of unemployment
moves.what: Recalls the model: an economy turns raw material, technology, capital and labour into output called GDP.

moves.concept: natural rate of unemployment
moves.what: Even when the economy produces its maximum GDP, some percentage of people stay unemployed: that is the natural rate.

moves.concept: natural rate of unemployment
moves.what: Iska matlab: in the long run, however much you raise inflation, unemployment cannot go below the natural rate; restated with 'yaani'.

moves.concept: NAIRU: pushing below the natural rate only speeds up inflation
moves.what: If you try with monetary or fiscal policy, inflation shoots up but unemployment still does not fall.

moves.concept: NAIRU: pushing below the natural rate only speeds up inflation
moves.what: So the natural rate is also called NAIRU, yaani non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment, because going below it makes inflation jump.

moves.concept: NAIRU: pushing below the natural rate only speeds up inflation
moves.what: This deviation of the Phillips curve is the theory Friedman and Phelps gave.

moves.concept: NAIRU: pushing below the natural rate only speeds up inflation
moves.what: Today we understood the Phillips curve and its long-term variation.

narration.density: About seven concept terms (Phillips curve, inverse relation, trade-off, short term vs long term, natural rate, NAIRU, monetary/fiscal policy) plus about eight names, dates and titles in about 288 s. Concepts come at about 1.5 per minute, but the first 70 s is biography and trivia before the curve is read.

talmel_summary: The best fit is the dot on the curve: it climbs while bars on both axes grow and shrink, then slides back to the natural rate as the wage chain is written, and later sits still while push arrows and piling hatch lines show inflation speeding up. Here the picture truly shows the process. The biography leans on a real photo, a journal cover and notes that copy the speech; the wage chain is text only. Once the voice gives the wrong direction ('unemployment comes back down') while the picture moves the right way, and the recap is spoken over promo and the end screen.

voice.notes: About 178 words per minute, storyteller tone for the history (dates and names said slowly, the thesis title read in full English), then a steadier explaining tone for the curve. Uses 'basically' and 'yaani' to restate each rule in plainer Hinglish. Says the economists' names with titles ('Nobel laureate'). Misspeaks twice: unemployment 'wapas neeche aa jayega' where it should rise to the natural rate, and 'Edmond Phillips' for Phelps near the end.

game_ideas.player_does: Is the central bank and turns an inflation dial each year to cut unemployment.
game_ideas.process_happens: In the short run the dot climbs the curve and the unemployment bar shrinks; after a few years wage-demand cards play (prices up, workers ask for raises, firms cannot pay all, firing) and the dot slides back to the natural rate while inflation stays high; pushing harder piles up hatch lines without moving the dot.
game_ideas.win: Keep unemployment at the natural rate with steady inflation for ten years (find NAIRU).
game_ideas.lose: Pushing unemployment below the natural rate makes the inflation meter run away while unemployment returns, which teaches the long-run critique.
game_ideas.concept: short-run trade-off vs long-run natural rate (NAIRU)

game_ideas.player_does: Orders cards to explain why the trade-off breaks: high inflation, higher living costs, demand for higher wages, firms cannot pay everyone, firing, unemployment back to the natural rate.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each correct card moves the dot one step back along the curve and writes the step in the chain box.
game_ideas.win: Dot back at the natural rate with the chain complete.
game_ideas.lose: A card out of order freezes the dot and shows which earlier step is missing.
game_ideas.concept: why the trade-off fails in the long run

game_ideas.player_does: Places idea cards on a timeline: 1950s thesis on UK data, 1958 publication, 1960s fame, early 1970s challenge, natural rate and NAIRU.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each placed card changes the curve on screen: it appears, grows famous (gets a crown), gets a 'short term' label, then the label is struck and 'long term' and NAIRU appear.
game_ideas.win: Timeline complete and the final curve matches the video's last picture.
game_ideas.lose: Putting the challenge before the publication shows a crossed-out curve with nothing to challenge yet.
game_ideas.concept: the life of the Phillips curve idea

checks_learned: Direction words in the speech (badhna / ghatna / neeche / upar) must match the direction of the animated quantity at that moment; here the voice said unemployment comes down while the dot moved to higher unemployment.
The same date range must not be given two ways in one script (data 1861-1957 vs a title ending 1965) unless the difference is explained.
A person's name must be said the same way every time (Phelps later said as 'Phillips').
A term should be explained within about 15 s of being named; here the natural rate was named at 189 s and explained only at 216 s.
No end-card or promo overlay may start while teaching speech is still running, and the recap must sit on the final teaching picture.
When an acronym is expanded in speech (NAIRU), the expansion should be written beside it at the same time.
Trivia read aloud over a still frame (thesis title) should be cut or turned into a short note card.

teaching_best.why: A dot climbing the curve while both axis bars change makes the trade-off a movement the learner watches, not a sentence.
The critique is shown on the same curve: 'Short Term' is struck, 'long term' is written, and the dot slides back.
Push arrows squeeze a dot that will not move while hatch lines pile up: NAIRU is seen before it is named.
Telling the topic as an idea that was believed and then challenged gives the lesson a story arc and a reason to listen.

teaching_weak.why: About 55 s of biography, data years and the thesis title before the curve is read; a real photo carries much of it.
The voice says unemployment comes back down, contradicting both its own earlier line and the dot's movement.
Fame is shown by a journal-cover photo and a caption; nothing about the idea is shown.
The conclusion and recap are spoken while promo and the end screen take over the frame.
